The Story of Dharsenacharya

I bow to Lord Jina, whose omniscient knowledge is like a supreme eye, and I write the story of Acharya Dharsena, who was related to the preservation of scriptures through proper letters and words.

In a cave on Girnar Mountain, Acharya Shri Dharsena, who was like the moon for the ocean of Jain dharma, resided. Through his knowledge of omens, he realised that his lifespan was very short. Then he needed two students to whom he could teach some knowledge of the angas and other texts for the preservation of scriptural knowledge. The Acharya then sent a letter to Sanghadhipati Mahasenacharya, who had come to the city of Venatatt in Andhra Pradesh on a pilgrimage. In it, he wrote:

'May the teaching of Lord Mahavir remain firm, and may it spread throughout all lands. The reason for writing is this: although in this Kaliyug the knowledge of the angas will not remain, still, for the preservation of scriptural knowledge, please send me two such intelligent students who are very sharp in intellect, steady, patient, and capable of upholding Jain doctrine.'

The Acharya gave the letter to a brahmachari and sent him to Mahasenacharya. Mahasenacharya was very pleased to read the letter. He then sent two dharma-loving monks, Pushpadant and Bhutabali, who were capable of upholding the doctrine, from his sangha to Dharsenacharya with great love.

On the night before the day these two monks were to arrive at the Acharya's place, Dharsenacharya had a dream. In the dream, he saw two healthy, well-built, white bulls bowing at his feet with great devotion. Seeing this auspicious dream, the Acharya's joy was beyond description. He rose saying, 'May the Shrutedevi, the word of Jina, which destroys all doubts, always be victorious in this world forever.'

At dawn, the two monks he had been waiting for came and bowed their heads at the Acharya's feet with great devotion, praising him. The Acharya then blessed them: 'May you live long and serve the pure teaching of Lord Mahavir. Give knowledge to worldly souls who have become slaves to ignorance and sensual pleasures, and engage them in their duty. Remind them of their dharma and their true nature.'

Through the Acharya's teaching, Pushpadant and Bhutabali preserved and propagated the Jain scriptures. They composed important works that ensured the survival of Jain doctrine for future generations. Their efforts, guided by Dharsenacharya's wisdom, protected the sacred knowledge from being lost in the dark ages.

This story teaches the importance of preserving sacred knowledge through proper transmission. Acharya Dharsena, knowing his time was short, sought worthy students to carry forward the tradition. The two monks he chose — Pushpadant and Bhutabali — through their dedication and scholarship, ensured that Jain scriptures survived for posterity. The wise should understand that knowledge must be carefully preserved and transmitted to worthy successors.
